section.title: One-sided limits and infinite behavior
section.p: Section gave us tools for limits that settle down to a finite number. But limits can fail, or change character, in several different ways.

A graph can approach one value from the left and another from the right. A function can grow without bound near a point. Or the input itself can move farther and farther away, so that we ask what happens at the far ends of the graph.
These are not rare exceptions. They are some of the most important behaviors calculus has to name.

subsection.title: Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes
subsection.p: A limit can fail in a different way. The left and right sides might agree in direction, but the values might not settle near any finite number.
Consider
As x gets close to 2, the denominator (x-2)^2 gets close to 0, but it remains positive. Dividing 1 by a very small positive number gives a very large positive number.
The values do not approach a finite number. They grow beyond any fixed bound.
We write
This notation needs careful reading. The symbol \infty is not a real number. So this is not a finite limit. It is a way of saying that the function grows without bound.

subsection.p: The sign matters. Now consider
If x\gt 2, then x-2\gt 0, so g(x)\gt 0. As x\to 2^+, the denominator is a small positive number, so g(x)\to\infty.
If x\lt 2, then x-2\lt 0, so g(x)\lt 0. As x\to 2^-, the denominator is a small negative number, so g(x)\to-\infty.

subsection.p: The vertical line x=2 is called a vertical asymptote.

statement.p: The line x=a is a vertical asymptote of the graph of f if at least one of the one-sided limits \lim_{x\to a^-}f(x) or \lim_{x\to a^+}f(x) is \infty or -\infty.

subsection.title: Limits at infinity
subsection.p: So far, the input x has approached a finite number. But many questions ask what happens after a long time, far from the starting point, or for very large input.
For example, suppose the temperature of a cup of coffee in a room is modeled by
where T(t) is measured in degrees Fahrenheit and t is measured in hours.
At the start,
As t grows, the fraction \frac{90}{t+1} gets smaller. The temperature approaches 70, the room temperature.
We write
The notation t\to\infty does not mean that t approaches a number called infinity. It means that t grows without bound.

statement.p: We write \lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=L if f(x) approaches L as x becomes arbitrarily large.
We write \lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)=L if f(x) approaches L as x becomes negative with arbitrarily large magnitude.

subsection.p: When the numerator has larger degree, the function may grow like a polynomial. Sometimes it grows close to a line. That leads to slant asymptotes.

subsection.title: Horizontal and slant asymptotes
subsection.p: A horizontal asymptote describes the far end of a graph.

statement.p: If \lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=L or \lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)=L, then the line y=L is a horizontal asymptote of the graph of f on that end.

subsection.p: For the coffee model T(t)=70+\frac{90}{t+1}, we have \lim_{t\to\infty}T(t)=70. So the graph has horizontal asymptote T=70. That asymptote has a physical meaning: it is the room temperature.

Some graphs do not approach a horizontal line. Instead, they approach a tilted line.

subsection.p: The important quantity is not the ratio of f(x) to the line. It is the vertical difference: f(x)-(mx+b). If that difference approaches 0, the graph approaches the line.
